headline: Captree dock talk: fluke scattered, bass sleeping, but the bunker are stacking up for fall
subhead: Warm water has the flatties spread thin and the bass in a holding pattern, but the bait building along the beach says the turn is closer than the calendar suggests.
body_markdown:
Had a mate leaning on the rail at the Captree docks Tuesday morning, coffee in hand, telling anyone who'd listen that he'd run six drifts off the west end of Robert Moses and boxed exactly one keeper fluke for his trouble. "They're out there," he said, "just not together anymore." That about sums up the week on this end of the South Shore, and it's not a mystery why.

Water's been sitting warm — 71 degrees plus out on the ocean side, and the bay's held that heat right through the back channels. Fluke don't love that. When the flats get warm and thin on oxygen, the fish stop schooling up tight and start spreading out looking for anything cooler, which is exactly what's happened from the Robert Moses bridges down through Nicoll Bay. The bite hasn't died, it's just gotten lazy and scattered — the fish that are biting are holding on channel edges and current-scoured structure where there's a cooler bottom layer to sit in, not out on the open flats where they were stacked in June and July.

That means the west channel around the Robert Moses bridge pilings, the deeper cuts off Democrat Point, and the drop-offs along the edges of the Fire Island Inlet channel are still worth your gas money. Boats working 25 to 35 feet on the last two hours of the outgoing, dragging white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails or bouncing a Fluke Ball rig tipped with squid strips, have been picking through shorts to find keepers to five and six pounds. It's not a fast bite. It's a patient one — cover ground, find the seam where the current's still moving good water, and stick with it instead of running all over the bay chasing yesterday's report.

Striped bass are doing what late August stripers do around here — going quiet in the heat of the day and turning on after dark. Daytime action inside the bay and off the beach has been spotty at best, mostly cocktail-sized fish mixed with the bluefish on structure, but the real story is what's staging up off the beach. Bunker schools have been thickening up along the south shore beaches from Cedar Beach out toward Gilgo, and that's not nothing this time of year. We flagged this last week — said the pattern would sharpen as the moon swung toward full — and here we are, one day out from the full moon on the 28th, with those bunker schools tightening exactly like we said they would. Guys snagging bait off the beach and running it live through the inlet on the last of the incoming have connected with better fish, slot-class and a few overslots, working the seam where the inlet current meets the open bay just inside Democrat Point. That's your night program right now: livelined bunker, fished on circle hooks in 15 to 20 feet, right on that current edge as the tide turns.

Bluefish have been the one constant nobody's complaining about. Snapper blues are thick in the docks around Patchogue and Sayville — kids with bobbers and spearing are having a field day — while the adult cocktail blues are mixing into the fluke drifts and the structure bites out at the inlet, hammering diamond jigs and bucktails meant for something else entirely. If you want a guaranteed bend in the rod for a couple hours, that's still the move.

Here's the one to watch: the first scouting reports on false albacore are starting to trickle in from the inlet rips and the deeper cuts in the Great South Bay, right on schedule for the tail end of August. Rainfish and spearing are tightening up along the beach and in the bay rips, which is exactly the bait signature that pulls albies in tight to the structure. Nobody's called a real bite yet — it's a handful of boils and a few guys getting bit off — but with the moon building and the tides about to swing bigger, this is the week that pattern usually goes from rumor to real. Small Deadly Dicks and epoxy jigs worked fast through the froth at Democrat Point or the east end rips off Smith Point would be the first thing I'd tie on if that bite shows itself.

Looking ahead, the moon goes full on the 28th, which means bigger water movement through the inlet and sharper, shorter bite windows everywhere from Robert Moses to Patchogue. Wind's holding out of the southwest in that 8 to 12 knot range, keeping the ocean manageable and the water clean. If you've only got one shot this week, make it the last two hours of the incoming at the inlet after dark for bass, or the outgoing at the bridge pilings for fluke — and keep an eye on the horizon for that first real albie blitz. The bait's building. The rest usually follows.
